rv.q: This is both a dizzying descriptive tapestry and merrily defiant celebration of a many-shaded self.

While she steers the show with the bright smile of a good missionary spreading the gospel of going beyond the binary, the cheerful profanity of The Least Problematic Woman becomes its own constriction.
The Least Problematic Woman in the World is a 90-minute joy bomb.
The Least Problematic Woman in the World is not without flaws—but like its creator, it dares to be seen in all its contradictions.
The Least Problematic Woman in the World is a campy, frothy good time with real heart.
The new title is a better fit, since Mulvaney mostly works hard to charm and amuse and entertain us.
Though she’s still young, Mulvaney has so much to tell us, and there’s no possible way to cram it into 75 minutes.
Her infectious joy brightens the entire theater, transporting the audience to a space without worry of judgment and scrutiny, a skill honed, Mulvaney explains, by her social media career.
It's a whole lot of fun — fearless, funny, and deeply human.
It was flashy, glitzy, glamorous, and irreverent— and it was also touching, raw, emotional, real, and utterly transformative.
Mulvaney's messy, marvelous, madcap life—and the show it inspired—are all the better for it.
It’s a beautiful day in her gayborhood, and The Least Problematic Woman in the World is the most fabulous block party around.
Broadly engaging, this autobiographical show succeeds where others of this ilk often fail.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace Mulvaney's campy, glitter-filled solo show as a vulnerable yet joyful autobiographical spectacle, praising its high production values and sincerity beneath the irony, though some find it overly theatrical.
